la:verb:attendo.gloss: to pay attention, attend (to), direct the attention towards
senses: to pay attention, attend (to), direct the attention towards
la:verb:attendo.html:
attendo (adt-, Dietsch), tendi, tentum, 3, v. a., orig.,
to stretch something (e. g. the bow) toward something; so only in Appul.: arcum, Met. 2, p. 122, 5.—Hence,
In gen., to direct or turn toward, = advertere, admovere: aurem, Att. ap. ; Trag. Rel. p. 173 Rib. (cf. infra, P. a.): attendere signa ad aliquid,i. e. to affix, (Halm, aptare); so, manus caelo, to stretch or extend toward, : caput eodem attentum,.—Far more freq.,
Trop.
Animum or animos attendere, or absol. attendere, also animo attendere, to direct the attention, apply the mind to something, to attend to, consider, mind, give heed to (cf.: advertere animum, and animadvertere; freq. and class.)
With animum or animos: animum ad quaerendum quid siet, Pac. ap. : dictis animum, Lucil. ib.: animum coepi attendere,: quo tempore aures judex erigeret animumque attenderet?: si, cum animum attenderis, turpitudinem videas, etc.,: animum ad cavendum, Nep Alcib 5, 2: jubet peritos linguae attendere animum, pastorum sermo agresti an urbano propior esset,: praeterea et nostris animos attendere dictis atque adhibere velis, Lucil. ap. : attendite animos ad ea, quae consequuntur,.—With a rel.-clause as object: nunc quid velim, animum attendite,.—
Absol.: postquam attendi Magis et vi coepi cogere, ut etc.,: rem gestam vobis dum breviter expono, quaeso, diligenter attendite,: audi, audi atque attende,; so ; ; ; —With acc. of the thing or person to which the attention is directed: Glaucia solebat populum monere, ut, cum lex aliqua recitaretur, primum versum attenderet,: sed stuporem hominis attendite,mark the stupidity,; so ; ; ; : me de invidiosis rebus dicentem attendite. ; : Quā re attendo te studiose,: non attenderunt mandata, Esdr. 9, 34; ib. Job, 21, 5; .— Pass.: versūs aeque prima et media et extrema pars attenditur,. —With inf. or acc. and inf. as object: quid futurum est, si pol ego hanc discere artem attenderim? Pompon. ap. : non attendere superius illud eā re a se esse concessum,.—With a rel.clause or a subjunct. with a particle: cum attendo, quā prudentiā sit Hortensius,: Hermagoras nec, quid dicat, attendere nec ... videatur,: forte lubuit adtendere, quae res maxume tanta negotia sustinuisset,: Oro, parumper Attendas, quantum de legibus queratur etc.,: attende, cur, etc.,: attendite ut sciatis prudentiam,: Attendite, ne justitiam vestram faciatis etc.,; ; ; .— With de: cum de necessitate attendemus,.—With dat. (post-Aug.): sermonibus malignis,: cui magis quam Caesari attendant?; : attendit mandatis,; : attendite vobis,take heed to yourselves,; ; .—So in Suet. several times in the signif. to devote attention to, to study, = studere: eloquentiae plurimum attendit,: juri,: extispicio,.—With abl. with ab (after the Gr. προσέχειν ἀπό τινος; eccl. Lat.): attende tibi a pestifero,beware of,: attendite ab omni iniquo,; ; ; .—
With animo (ante- and post-class. and rare): cum animo attendi ad quaerendum, Pac., Trag. Rel. p. 79 Rib.: nunc quid petam, aequo animo attendite,: quid istud sit, animo attendatis,: ut magis magisque attendant animo, prol.; so, in verbis meis attende in corde tuo,.—*
To strive eagerly for something, long for: puer, ne attenderis Petere a me id quod nefas sit concedi tibi, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 173 Rib.).—Hence, attentus, a, um, P. a.
Directed to something, attentive, intent on: Ut animus in spe attentus fuit,: Quo magis attentas aurīs animumque reposco,: Verba per attentam non ibunt Caesaris aurem,: si attentos animos ad decoris conservationem tenebimus,: cum respiceremus attenti ad gentem,: eaque dum animis attentis admirantes excipiunt,: acerrima atque attentissima cogitatio,a very acute and close manner of thinking,: et attentum monent Graeci a principio faciamus judicem et docilem,; 2, 19, 80; ; Auct. ad : Ut patris attenti, lenonis ut insidiosi,: judex circa jus attentior,.—
Intent on, striving after something, careful, frugal, industrious: unum hoc vitium fert senectus hominibus: Attentiores sumus ad rem omnes quam sat est,: nimium ad rem in senectā attente sumus,: tum enim cum rem habebas, quaesticulus te faciebat attentiorem,: paterfamilias et prudens et attentus,: Durus, ait, Voltei, nimis attentusque videris Esse mihi,: asper et attentus quaesitis,: vita, Matth.: qui in re adventiciā et hereditariā tam diligens, tam attentus esset,: antiqui attenti continentiae,.—Comp.: hortor vos attentiori studio lectionem facere, * prol.—Hence, adv.: atten-tē, attentively, carefully, etc.: attente officia servorum fungi,; audire,; ; ; : legere,: parum attente dicere,: custodire attente,.— Comp.: attentius audire,: acrius et attentius cogitare,: attentius agere aliquid,: spectare,: invicem diligere, Pet 1, 22.—Sup.: attentissime audire,.

la:conj:at.gloss: introduces a different but not completely opposing thought: but, yet, moreover, on the other hand, on the contrary, still
senses: introduces a different but not completely opposing thought: but, yet, moreover, on the other hand, on the contrary, still
la:conj:at.html:
at or ast,
conj. [Curtius connects the Sanscr. ati, ultra, nimis, the Gr. ἔτι, the Lat. et, and at in atavus; Vanicek connects with these at, atque, and atqui. Thus the original idea of addition is prominent in ἔτι, et, and atque; and the idea of opposition in at and atqui, which agree with ἀτ-άρ in meaning as well as in form. After the same analogy, the Gr. πλέον, more, has become πλήν, but; and the Lat. magis has passed into the same meaning in the Fr. mais and the Ital. mai. The confusion in MSS. between at, ac, and et, and between atque and atqui, was prob. caused as much by their connection in idea as in form] (it was sometimes, for the sake of euphony, written ad; cf. ; ; ; P., where, instead of at conjunctionem esse, ad vero praepositionem, the reading should be, ad conjunctionem esse, at vero praepositionem, Fr.; v. the pass. in its connection; cf. also Vel. Long. p. 2230 P.; P.; Mar. Vict. p. 2458 P. The form ast is found in the old laws; it occurs once in Trag. Rel., but never in Com. Rel. nor in Lucil.; at is found in Plautus about 280 times, and ast about 10 times; in Ter. at about 100 times, and ast once; in Hor. at 60 times, ast 3 times; in Verg. at 168 times, ast 16; in Juv. at 17 times, ast 7; Catull., Tibull., and Prop. use only at, and Pers. (Jahn) only ast; in prose, Cic. uses

ast in his epistles. It joins to a previous thought a new one, either antithetical or simply different, and especially an objection; while sed denotes a direct opposition; and autem marks a transition, and denotes at once a connection and an opposition).

In adding a diff., but not entirely opp. thought, a qualification, restriction, etc., moreover, but, yet; sometimes an emphasized (but never merely copulative) and.
In gen.: SEI PARENTEM PVER VERBERIT AST OLE PLORASSIT PVER DIVEIS PARENTOM SACER ESTO, if the son strike his father, and the father complain, let the son, etc., Lex Serv. Tullii ap. Fest. s. v. plorare, p. 230 Müll.; Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. : Philosophari est mihi necesse, at paucis, but only in a few words, Enn., Trag. Rel. p. 65 Rib.: DIVOS ET EOS QVI CAELESTES, SEMPER HABITI COLVNTO ... AST OLLA PROPTER QVAE etc.,; : hinc Remus auspicio se devovet atque secundam Solus avem servat. At Romulus pulcer in alto Quaerit Aventino, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 83 Vahl.); : si ego hic peribo, ast ille, ut dixit, non redit,: paret Amor dictis carae genetricis. At Venus Ascanio placidam per membra quietem Inrigat,: (Aeneas) finem dedit ore loquendi. At, Phoebi nondum patiens, immanis in antro Bacchatur vates,; 11, 709 sq.: quo (odore) totum nati corpus perduxit; at illi Dulcis compositis spiravit crinibus aura,; so ; 4, 513; ; ; ; 8, 241; 9, 793; ; ; ; —Also in prose (chiefly post-Aug.): una (navis) cum Nasidianis profugit: at ex reliquis una praemissa Massiliam, etc.,: ubi facta sunt, in unum omnia miscentur. At pastilli haec ratio est, etc.,; : quamquam insideret urbem proprius miles, tres urbanae, novem praetoriae cohortes Etruriā ferme Umbriāque delectae aut vetere Latio et coloniis antiquitus Romanis. At apud idonea provinciarum sociae triremes etc.,; : negavit aliā se condicione adlecturum, quam si pateretur ascribi albo, extortum sibi a matre. At illa commota etc.,; ; ; ; ; —In the enumeration of particulars: Cum alio cantat, at tamen alii suo dat digito litteras, Naev., Com. Rel. p. 20 Rib.: dant alios aliae (silvae) fetus: dant utile lignum Navigiis pinos ... At myrtus validis hastilibus et bona bello Cornus,: Nam neque tum stellis acies obtunsa videtur ... At nebulae magis etc.,; 3, 87; : Hic altā Sicyone, ast hic Amydone relictā, Hic Andro, etc.,.— The Vulg. often uses at as a mere continuative, where even et or atque might stand: sciscitabur ab iis ubi Christus nasceretur. At illi dixerunt ei: In etc., Matt. 2, 5; 4, 20; 8, 32; 14, 29; 15, 34 et persaep.—In transition,
Esp.,
To a new narration, like the Gr. δέ; so the commencement of the fourth book of the Æneid: At regina gravi jam dudum saucia curā, etc. (the third book closes with the narrative of Æneas); so the beginning of the third book of the Thebaid of Statius: At non Aoniae moderator perfidus aulae, etc.; ; ; ; 5, 700; 5, 779; 6, 679; 7, 5; 8, 370; 8, 608; 9, 503; 10, 689; 11, 597; 12, 134 et saep.—Also in the postAug. histt. and other prose writers; so after speaking of the Ubii etc., Tac. says: At in Chaucis coeptavere seditionem praesidium agitantes etc., A. 1, 38; so ; ; et saep.—
To a wonderful, terrible, unexpected, or exciting occurrence or circumstance: clamores simul horrendos ad sidera tollit, etc. ... At gemini lapsu delubra ad summa dracones Effugiunt,; : Lacte madens illic suberat Pan ilicis umbrae, Et facta agresti lignea falce Pales etc. At quā Velabri regio patet etc.,; : consurgit Turnus in ensem et ferit. Exclamant Troes trepidique Latini, Arrectaeque amborum acies. At perfidus ensis Frangitur in medio,; : adusque Supremum tempus, ne se penuria victūs Opprimeret metuebat. At hunc liberta securi divisit medium,: Magnus quanto mucrone minatur Noctibus hibernis et sidera terret Orion. At sonipes habitus etc., .—
To a passionate appeal, etc., in which case the antecedent clause is not expressed, but must be considered as existing in the mind of the speaker; cf. in Gr. ἀλλὰ σύ, σὺ δέ.
In passing to an interrogation, exhortation, request: At, scelesta, viden ut ne id quidem me dignum esse existumat?; : At qui nummos tristis inuncat? Müll.: Me. Sauream non novi. Li. At nosce sane, : Ca. Non adest. Ps. At tu cita, : satis habeo, at quaeso hercle etiam vide, (Ritschl, sat habeo. Sed): at unum hoc quaeso ... Ut, etc.,: at tu, qui laetus rides mala nostra caveto Mox tibi,: Hunc ut Peleus vidit, At inferias, juvenum gratissime Crantor, Accipe, ait,: at tu, nauta, vagae ne parce malignus arenae Ossibus et capiti inhumato Particulam dare,.—In prose: at vide quid succenseat,: itaque pulsus ego civitate non sum, quae nulla erat: at vide, quam ista tui latrocinii tela contempserim,; ; .—
In expressions of passion, astonishment, indignation, pain, etc.: At ut scelesta sola secum murmurat,: Sc. Nunc quidem domi certost: certa res est Nunc nostrum opservare ostium, [ubi] ubist. Pa. At, Sceledre, quaeso, Ut etc., : At o deorum quidquid in caelo regit Terras et humanum genus, Quid iste fert tumultus?: At tibi quanta domus rutila testudine fulgens, etc.,.—In prose: horum omnium studium una mater oppugnat: at quae mater?; : at per deos immortales! quid est, quod de hoc dici possit,: institui senatores, qui omnia indicum responsa perscriberent. At quos viros!; : tangit et ira deos: at non impune feremus,; : at tibi Colchorum, memini, regina vacavi,.—
In indignant imprecations: At te di omnes cum consilio, Calve, mactāssint malo! Pomp., Com. Rel. p. 245 Rib.: At te Juppiter diique omnes perdant!: At te di deaeque faxint cum isto odio, Laches,: At te di perdant,: At tibi di dignum factis exitium duint,: At vobis male sit,: At tibi, pro scelere, exclamat, pro talibus ausis Di ... persolvant grates dignas et praemia reddant Debita!.—In prose: At vos, ait, devota capita, respiciant di perjuriorum vindices,.—
Rarely of friendly inclination, disposition: At tibi di bene faciant omnes,: At tibi di semper, adulescens, quisquis es, faciant bene,: At tu, Catulle, destinatus obdura,.—
In entreaty: At vos, o superi, miserescite regis,: at tu, pater deūm hominumque, hinc saltem arce hostes,.—
In adding an entirely opposite thought, but, but indeed, but on the other hand, on the contrary, etc. (the strictly class. signif. of the word).
In gen.: at differentiam rerum significat: ut cum dicimus, Scipio est bellator, at M. Cato orator, Paul. ex Müll.: splendet saepe, ast idem nimbis interdum nigret, Att., Trag. Rel. p. 170 Rib.: So. Mentire nunc. Me. At jam faciam, ut verum dicas dicere, : So. Per Jovem juro med etc. Me. At ego per Mercurium juro, tibi etc., : Atque oppido hercle bene velle illud visus sum, Ast non habere quoi commendarem caprum,: fecit idem Themistocles ... at idem Pericles non fecit,: non placet M. Antonio consulatus meus, at placuit P. Servilio,: majores nostri Tusculanos Aequos ... in civitatem etiam acceperunt, at Karthaginem et Numantiam funditus sustulerunt,: brevis a naturā nobis vita data est; at memoria bene redditae vitae sempiterna,; ; : crebras a nobis litteras exspecta, ast plures etiam ipse mittito,: Rejectis pilis comminus gladiis pugnatum est. At Germani phalange factā impetus gladiorum exceperunt, Caes. B. G. 1, 52: Postquam Caesar dicendi finem fecit, ceteri verbo alius alii varie adsentiebantur. At M. Porcius Cato hujusce modi orationem habuit,: hac iter Elysium nobis, at laeva ... ad impia Tartara mittit,: T. Ante leves ergo pascentur in aethere cervi ... M. At nos hinc alii sitientīs ibimus Afros, : Dam. Malo me Galatea petit, lasciva puella ... Men. At mihi sese offert ultro meus ignis Amyntas, ; 7, 35; 7, 55; ; ; ; 2, 151; 2, 184; 3, 331; 4, 18; 4, 180; ; ; ; 5, 264; 6, 489: Ast ego nutrici non mando vota,: ast illi tremat etc.,: Ast vocat officium,: At Jesus audiens ait,; ; ; 12, 48 et persaep.—
In order to strengthen a contrast, sometimes (esp. in Plaut. and Ter.) with contra, e contrario, potius, etiam, vero.
With contra: Summis nitere opibus, at ego contra ut dissimilis siem, Müll.: Ergo quod magnumst aeque leviusque videtur ... At contra gravius etc.,; so ; ; : L. Opimius ejectus est e patriā: At contra bis Catilina absolutus est, ; ; ; : At tibi contra Evenit, etc.,: (Cornutus) taedio curarum mortem in se festinavit: at contra reus nihil infracto animo, etc.,.—
With e contrario: apud nos mercenarii scribae existimantur; at apud illos e contrario nemo ad id officium admittitur, nisi, etc.,: in locis siccis partibus sulcorum imis disponenda sunt semina, ut tamquam in alveolis maneant. At uliginosis e contrario in summo porcae dorso collocanda, etc.,.—
With potius: at satius fuerat eam viro dare nuptum potius,: at potius serves nostram, tua munera, vitam,.—
With etiam: At etiam, furcifer, Male loqui mi audes? but do you even? etc., ; ; : At etiam cubat cuculus. Surge, amator, i domum,but he is yet abed,; so ; : Exi foras, sceleste. At etiam restitas, Fugitive!; : Proinde aut exeant, aut quiescant, etc. ... at etiam sunt, Quirites, qui dicant, a me in exsilium ejectum esse Catilinam, on the contrary, there are indeed people who say. etc., ; ; ; ; —(ε) With vero, but certainly: At vero aut honoribus aucti aut etc.,; ; ; ; —(ζ) With certe: Numquam ego te, vitā frater amabilior, Aspiciam posthac. At certe semper amabo,; . —(η) So, quidem—at (very rare) = quidem —autem, .—
Ironically: Th. Quid valeam? Ly. At tu aegrota, si lubet, per me aetatem quidem, : at, credo, mea numina tandem Fessa jacent,; ; .—
Very freq. in adding an objection, from one's own mind or another's, against an assertion previously made, but, on the contrary, in opposition to this; sometimes, but one may say, it may be objected, and the like: Piscium magnam atque altilium vim interfecisti. At nego, Müll.: Quid tandem te impedit? Mosne majorum? At persaepe etiam privati in hac re publicā perniciosos cives morte multārunt. An leges, quae de civium Romanorum supplicio rogatae sunt? At numquam in hac urbe etc.,: Appellandi tempus non erat? At tecum plus annum vixit. In Galliā agi non potuit? At et in provinciā jus dicebatur et etc.,: Male judicavit populus. At judicavit. Non debuit. At potuit. Non fero. At multi clarissimi cives tulerunt,: sunt, quos signa, quos caelatum argentum delectant. At sumus, inquiunt, civitatis principes,; ; : quid porro quaerendum est? Factumne sit? At constat: A quo? At patet,; : convivium vicinorum cotidie compleo, quod ad multam noctem, quam maxime possumus, vario sermone producimus. At non est voluptatum tanta quasi titillatio in senibus. Credo: sed ne desideratio quidem,

: multo magnus orator praestat minutis imperatoribus. At prodest plus imperator. Quis negat?; ; ; : Maxime Juppiter! At in se Pro quaestu sumptum facit hic,— In this case freq. strengthened,

By pol, edepol, hercule: At pol ego neque florem neque flocces volo mihi, Caecil., Com. Rel. p. 67 Rib.: So. Non edepol volo profecto. Me. At pol profecto ingratiis, ; so ; ; ; ; ; : Ha. Gaudio ero vobis. Ad. At edepol nos voluptati tibi, ; : At hercule aliquot annos populus Romanus maximā parte imperii caruit,; : at hercle in eā controversiā, quae de Argis est, superior sum,: At, Hercule, reliquis omnibus etc.,: At, hercules, Diodorus et in morbo etc.,: At hercule Germanicum Druso ortum etc.,; ; ; 3, 54: At, hercules, si conscius fuissem etc.,—
By enim, which introduces a reason for the objection implied in at, but certainly, but surely, but indeed, etc., ἀλλὰ γάρ: At enim tu nimis spisse incedis, Naev., Com. Rel. p. 16 Rib.; Turp. : at enim nimis hic longo sermone utimur; Diem conficimus,: At enim istoc nil est magis etc.,: At enim vereor, inquit Crassus, ne haec etc.,: cum dixisset Sophocles, O puerum pulchrum, Pericle. At enim praetorem, Sophocle, decet non solum manus, sed etiam oculos abstinentes habere, etc., Beier; so ; : at enim inter hos ipsos existunt graves controversiae,; so ; ; ; : At enim cur a me potissimum hoc praesidium petiverunt?: At enim quis reprehendet, quod in parricidas rei publicae decretum erit? Kritz: At enim quid ita solus ego circum curam ago?; : At enim eo foedere, quod etc.,; ; : At enim nova nobis in fratrum filias conjugia; sed etc.,.—
By tamen: Jam id peccatum primum magnum, magnum, at humanum tamen, : Hi secretis sermonibus ... conveniunt; nam publice civitas talibus inceptis abhorrebat. At tamen interfuere quidam etc.,: At certe tamen, inquiunt, quod etc.,.—
With a preced. negative, sometimes no antithesis is appended by at, but it is indicated that if what has been said is not true, yet at least something else is true, but yet; sometimes with tamen, but yet; or certe, but at least, yet at least: Nolo victumas: at minimis me extis placare volo,: Si tibi non cordi fuerant conubia nostra, ... At tamen in vostras potuisti ducere sedes,: Non cognoscebantur foris, at domi: non ab alienis, at a suis,: Liceat haec nobis, si oblivisci non possumus, at tacere,: Si genus humanum et mortalia temnitis arma, At sperate deos memores fandi atque nefandi,; so , and 6, 406. —With certe: Haec erant ... quorum cognitio studiosis juvenibus si non magnam utilitatem adferet, at certe, quod magis petimus, bonam voluntatem,; ; , al.—
The antithesis is sometimes not so much in the clause appended by at, as in the persons or things introduced in it; so,
Esp. freq. in conditional clauses with si, si non, si minus, etiam si, etc.; cf. Herm. ad Viger. 241: Si ego hic peribo, ast ille, ut dixit, non redit; At erit mi hoc factum mortuo memorabile, if I perish here, but he does not return, yet etc., ; : si ego digna hac contumeliā Sum maxime, at tu indignus qui faceres tamen,: Si tu oblitus es, at di meminerunt,: si non eo die, at postridie,: si non paulo, at aliquanto (post petīsses),; ; : quanta tempestas invidiae nobis, si minus in praesens, at in posteritatem impendeat,; ; : qui non possit, etiam si sine ullā suspitione, at non sine argumento male dicere, .—
With etsi: ei, etsi nequāquam parem illius ingenio, at pro nostro tamen studio meritam gratiam referamus,; .—
With quod si: Quod si nihil cum potentiore juris humani relinquitur inopi, at ego ad deos confugiam,; .—
At, like autem and δέ, sometimes serves simply to introduce an explanation: cum Sic mutilus miniteris. At illi foeda cicatrix etc., now an ugly scar etc., . —
And also like δέ in Hom. and Hdt., it sometimes introduces an apodosis,
With si: Bellona, si hobie nobis victoriam duis, ast ego templum tibi voveo, if to-day thou bestow victory, then I etc., ἐάν—δέ, .—
With quoniam: Nunc, quoniam tuum insanabile ingenium est, at tu tuo supplicio doce etc., since your disposition is past cure, at least etc., ἐπεί—δέ, .!*?
At is sometimes repeated at the beginning of several clauses,
In opposition each to the preceding clause: Soph. Tu quidem haut etiam octoginta's pondo. Paegn. At confidentiā Militia illa militatur multo magis quam pondere. At ego hanc operam perdo, : Si ego hic peribo, ast ille, ut dixit, non redit: At erit mi hoc factum mortuo memorabile,; sqq. (Cic., in Quir. 7 and 10, opposes at to sed, and Tac., in A. 12, 6, sed to at).—
In opposition to some common clause preceding: At etiam asto? At etiam cesso foribus facere hisce assulas?: Quid tum esse existimas judicatum? Certe gratīs judicāsse. At condemnārat; at causam totam non audierat; at in contionibus etc.,: Sit flagitiorum omnium princeps: at est bonus imperator, at felix,; ; B. and K.: Nefarius Hippias Pisistrati filius arma contra patriam ferens; at Sulla, at Marius, at Cinna recte, imo jure fortasse,: At non formosa est, at non bene culta puella; At, puto, non votis saepe petita meis? Merk.: At quam sunt similes, at quam formosus uterque!: rideri possit eo quod Rusticius tonso toga defluit: at est bonus ut melior vir Non alius quisquam; at tibi amicus; at ingenium ingens Inculto latet hoc sub corpore, sqq. (cf. sed— sed,; ; ; and a similar use of ἀλλά in Hellenistic Greek, as ἀλλά—ἀλλά, 2 Cor. 2, 17: ἀλλά—ἀλλά —ἀλλά, 1 Cor. 6, 11).—
Though regularly occupying the first place in its clause or sentence, it sometimes stands second (cf. atque fin.): Saepius at si me, Lycida formose, revisas,; : Tutior at quanto merx est in classe secundā,: Mentior at si quid, etc.,: Gramineis ast inde toris discumbitur,: Major at inde etc.,.—See more upon this word in Hand, Turs. I. pp. 417-451; Wagner, Quaest. XXXVII. ad Verg. IV. pp. 581- 585.

Rel. nor in Lucil.; at is found in Plautus about 280 times, and ast about 10 times; in Ter. at about 100 times, and ast once; in Hor. at 60 times, ast 3 times; in Verg. at 168 times, ast 16; in Juv. at 17 times, ast 7; Catull., Tibull., and Prop. use only at, and Pers. (Jahn) only ast; in prose, Cic. uses

ast in his epistles. It joins to a previous thought a new one, either antithetical or simply different, and especially an objection; while sed denotes a direct opposition; and autem marks a transition, and denotes at once a connection and an opposition).

In adding a diff., but not entirely opp. thought, a qualification, restriction, etc., moreover, but, yet; sometimes an emphasized (but never merely copulative) and.
In gen.: SEI PARENTEM PVER VERBERIT AST OLE PLORASSIT PVER DIVEIS PARENTOM SACER ESTO, if the son strike his father, and the father complain, let the son, etc., Lex Serv. Tullii ap. Fest. s. v. plorare, p. 230 Müll.; Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. : Philosophari est mihi necesse, at paucis, but only in a few words, Enn., Trag. Rel. p. 65 Rib.: DIVOS ET EOS QVI CAELESTES, SEMPER HABITI COLVNTO ... AST OLLA PROPTER QVAE etc.,; : hinc Remus auspicio se devovet atque secundam Solus avem servat. At Romulus pulcer in alto Quaerit Aventino, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 83 Vahl.); : si ego hic peribo, ast ille, ut dixit, non redit,: paret Amor dictis carae genetricis. At Venus Ascanio placidam per membra quietem Inrigat,: (Aeneas) finem dedit ore loquendi. At, Phoebi nondum patiens, immanis in antro Bacchatur vates,; 11, 709 sq.: quo (odore) totum nati corpus perduxit; at illi Dulcis compositis spiravit crinibus aura,; so ; 4, 513; ; ; ; 8, 241; 9, 793; ; ; ; —Also in prose (chiefly post-Aug.): una (navis) cum Nasidianis profugit: at ex reliquis una praemissa Massiliam, etc.,: ubi facta sunt, in unum omnia miscentur. At pastilli haec ratio est, etc.,; : quamquam insideret urbem proprius miles, tres urbanae, novem praetoriae cohortes Etruriā ferme Umbriāque delectae aut vetere Latio et coloniis antiquitus Romanis. At apud idonea provinciarum sociae triremes etc.,; : negavit aliā se condicione adlecturum, quam si pateretur ascribi albo, extortum sibi a matre. At illa commota etc.,; ; ; ; ; —In the enumeration of particulars: Cum alio cantat, at tamen alii suo dat digito litteras, Naev., Com. Rel. p. 20 Rib.: dant alios aliae (silvae) fetus: dant utile lignum Navigiis pinos ... At myrtus validis hastilibus et bona bello Cornus,: Nam neque tum stellis acies obtunsa videtur ... At nebulae magis etc.,; 3, 87; : Hic altā Sicyone, ast hic Amydone relictā, Hic Andro, etc.,.— The Vulg. often uses at as a mere continuative, where even et or atque might stand: sciscitabur ab iis ubi Christus nasceretur. At illi dixerunt ei: In etc., Matt. 2, 5; 4, 20; 8, 32; 14, 29; 15, 34 et persaep.—In transition,
Esp.,
To a new narration, like the Gr. δέ; so the commencement of the fourth book of the Æneid: At regina gravi jam dudum saucia curā, etc. (the third book closes with the narrative of Æneas); so the beginning of the third book of the Thebaid of Statius: At non Aoniae moderator perfidus aulae, etc.; ; ; ; 5, 700; 5, 779; 6, 679; 7, 5; 8, 370; 8, 608; 9, 503; 10, 689; 11, 597; 12, 134 et saep.—Also in the postAug. histt. and other prose writers; so after speaking of the Ubii etc., Tac. says: At in Chaucis coeptavere seditionem praesidium agitantes etc., A. 1, 38; so ; ; et saep.—
To a wonderful, terrible, unexpected, or exciting occurrence or circumstance: clamores simul horrendos ad sidera tollit, etc. ... At gemini lapsu delubra ad summa dracones Effugiunt,; : Lacte madens illic suberat Pan ilicis umbrae, Et facta agresti lignea falce Pales etc. At quā Velabri regio patet etc.,; : consurgit Turnus in ensem et ferit. Exclamant Troes trepidique Latini, Arrectaeque amborum acies. At perfidus ensis Frangitur in medio,; : adusque Supremum tempus, ne se penuria victūs Opprimeret metuebat. At hunc liberta securi divisit medium,: Magnus quanto mucrone minatur Noctibus hibernis et sidera terret Orion. At sonipes habitus etc., .—
To a passionate appeal, etc., in which case the antecedent clause is not expressed, but must be considered as existing in the mind of the speaker; cf. in Gr. ἀλλὰ σύ, σὺ δέ.
In passing to an interrogation, exhortation, request: At, scelesta, viden ut ne id quidem me dignum esse existumat?; : At qui nummos tristis inuncat? Müll.: Me. Sauream non novi. Li. At nosce sane, : Ca. Non adest. Ps. At tu cita, : satis habeo, at quaeso hercle etiam vide, (Ritschl, sat habeo. Sed): at unum hoc quaeso ... Ut, etc.,: at tu, qui laetus rides mala nostra caveto Mox tibi,: Hunc ut Peleus vidit, At inferias, juvenum gratissime Crantor, Accipe, ait,: at tu, nauta, vagae ne parce malignus arenae Ossibus et capiti inhumato Particulam dare,.—In prose: at vide quid succenseat,: itaque pulsus ego civitate non sum, quae nulla erat: at vide, quam ista tui latrocinii tela contempserim,; ; .—
In expressions of passion, astonishment, indignation, pain, etc.: At ut scelesta sola secum murmurat,: Sc. Nunc quidem domi certost: certa res est Nunc nostrum opservare ostium, [ubi] ubist. Pa. At, Sceledre, quaeso, Ut etc., : At o deorum quidquid in caelo regit Terras et humanum genus, Quid iste fert tumultus?: At tibi quanta domus rutila testudine fulgens, etc.,.—In prose: horum omnium studium una mater oppugnat: at quae mater?; : at per deos immortales! quid est, quod de hoc dici possit,: institui senatores, qui omnia indicum responsa perscriberent. At quos viros!; : tangit et ira deos: at non impune feremus,; : at tibi Colchorum, memini, regina vacavi,.—
In indignant imprecations: At te di omnes cum consilio, Calve, mactāssint malo! Pomp., Com. Rel. p. 245 Rib.: At te Juppiter diique omnes perdant!: At te di deaeque faxint cum isto odio, Laches,: At te di perdant,: At tibi di dignum factis exitium duint,: At vobis male sit,: At tibi, pro scelere, exclamat, pro talibus ausis Di ... persolvant grates dignas et praemia reddant Debita!.—In prose: At vos, ait, devota capita, respiciant di perjuriorum vindices,.—
Rarely of friendly inclination, disposition: At tibi di bene faciant omnes,: At tibi di semper, adulescens, quisquis es, faciant bene,: At tu, Catulle, destinatus obdura,.—
In entreaty: At vos, o superi, miserescite regis,: at tu, pater deūm hominumque, hinc saltem arce hostes,.—
In adding an entirely opposite thought, but, but indeed, but on the other hand, on the contrary, etc. (the strictly class. signif. of the word).
In gen.: at differentiam rerum significat: ut cum dicimus, Scipio est bellator, at M. Cato orator, Paul. ex Müll.: splendet saepe, ast idem nimbis interdum nigret, Att., Trag. Rel. p. 170 Rib.: So. Mentire nunc. Me. At jam faciam, ut verum dicas dicere, : So. Per Jovem juro med etc. Me. At ego per Mercurium juro, tibi etc., : Atque oppido hercle bene velle illud visus sum, Ast non habere quoi commendarem caprum,: fecit idem Themistocles ... at idem Pericles non fecit,: non placet M. Antonio consulatus meus, at placuit P. Servilio,: majores nostri Tusculanos Aequos ... in civitatem etiam acceperunt, at Karthaginem et Numantiam funditus sustulerunt,: brevis a naturā nobis vita data est; at memoria bene redditae vitae sempiterna,; ; : crebras a nobis litteras exspecta, ast plures etiam ipse mittito,: Rejectis pilis comminus gladiis pugnatum est. At Germani phalange factā impetus gladiorum exceperunt, Caes. B. G. 1, 52: Postquam Caesar dicendi finem fecit, ceteri verbo alius alii varie adsentiebantur. At M. Porcius Cato hujusce modi orationem habuit,: hac iter Elysium nobis, at laeva ... ad impia Tartara mittit,: T. Ante leves ergo pascentur in aethere cervi ... M. At nos hinc alii sitientīs ibimus Afros, : Dam. Malo me Galatea petit, lasciva puella ... Men. At mihi sese offert ultro meus ignis Amyntas, ; 7, 35; 7, 55; ; ; ; 2, 151; 2, 184; 3, 331; 4, 18; 4, 180; ; ; ; 5, 264; 6, 489: Ast ego nutrici non mando vota,: ast illi tremat etc.,: Ast vocat officium,: At Jesus audiens ait,; ; ; 12, 48 et persaep.—
In order to strengthen a contrast, sometimes (esp. in Plaut. and Ter.) with contra, e contrario, potius, etiam, vero.
With contra: Summis nitere opibus, at ego contra ut dissimilis siem, Müll.: Ergo quod magnumst aeque leviusque videtur ... At contra gravius etc.,; so ; ; : L. Opimius ejectus est e patriā: At contra bis Catilina absolutus est, ; ; ; : At tibi contra Evenit, etc.,: (Cornutus) taedio curarum mortem in se festinavit: at contra reus nihil infracto animo, etc.,.—
With e contrario: apud nos mercenarii scribae existimantur; at apud illos e contrario nemo ad id officium admittitur, nisi, etc.,: in locis siccis partibus sulcorum imis disponenda sunt semina, ut tamquam in alveolis maneant. At uliginosis e contrario in summo porcae dorso collocanda, etc.,.—
With potius: at satius fuerat eam viro dare nuptum potius,: at potius serves nostram, tua munera, vitam,.—
With etiam: At etiam, furcifer, Male loqui mi audes? but do you even? etc., ; ; : At etiam cubat cuculus. Surge, amator, i domum,but he is yet abed,; so ; : Exi foras, sceleste. At etiam restitas, Fugitive!; : Proinde aut exeant, aut quiescant, etc. ... at etiam sunt, Quirites, qui dicant, a me in exsilium ejectum esse Catilinam, on the contrary, there are indeed people who say. etc., ; ; ; ; —(ε) With vero, but certainly: At vero aut honoribus aucti aut etc.,; ; ; ; —(ζ) With certe: Numquam ego te, vitā frater amabilior, Aspiciam posthac. At certe semper amabo,; . —(η) So, quidem—at (very rare) = quidem —autem, .—
Ironically: Th. Quid valeam? Ly. At tu aegrota, si lubet, per me aetatem quidem, : at, credo, mea numina tandem Fessa jacent,; ; .—
Very freq. in adding an objection, from one's own mind or another's, against an assertion previously made, but, on the contrary, in opposition to this; sometimes, but one may say, it may be objected, and the like: Piscium magnam atque altilium vim interfecisti. At nego, Müll.: Quid tandem te impedit? Mosne majorum? At persaepe etiam privati in hac re publicā perniciosos cives morte multārunt. An leges, quae de civium Romanorum supplicio rogatae sunt? At numquam in hac urbe etc.,: Appellandi tempus non erat? At tecum plus annum vixit. In Galliā agi non potuit? At et in provinciā jus dicebatur et etc.,: Male judicavit populus. At judicavit. Non debuit. At potuit. Non fero. At multi clarissimi cives tulerunt,: sunt, quos signa, quos caelatum argentum delectant. At sumus, inquiunt, civitatis principes,; ; : quid porro quaerendum est? Factumne sit? At constat: A quo? At patet,; : convivium vicinorum cotidie compleo, quod ad multam noctem, quam maxime possumus, vario sermone producimus. At non est voluptatum tanta quasi titillatio in senibus. Credo: sed ne desideratio quidem,

: multo magnus orator praestat minutis imperatoribus. At prodest plus imperator. Quis negat?; ; ; : Maxime Juppiter! At in se Pro quaestu sumptum facit hic,— In this case freq. strengthened,

By pol, edepol, hercule: At pol ego neque florem neque flocces volo mihi, Caecil., Com. Rel. p. 67 Rib.: So. Non edepol volo profecto. Me. At pol profecto ingratiis, ; so ; ; ; ; ; : Ha. Gaudio ero vobis. Ad. At edepol nos voluptati tibi, ; : At hercule aliquot annos populus Romanus maximā parte imperii caruit,; : at hercle in eā controversiā, quae de Argis est, superior sum,: At, Hercule, reliquis omnibus etc.,: At, hercules, Diodorus et in morbo etc.,: At hercule Germanicum Druso ortum etc.,; ; ; 3, 54: At, hercules, si conscius fuissem etc.,—
By enim, which introduces a reason for the objection implied in at, but certainly, but surely, but indeed, etc., ἀλλὰ γάρ: At enim tu nimis spisse incedis, Naev., Com. Rel. p. 16 Rib.; Turp. : at enim nimis hic longo sermone utimur; Diem conficimus,: At enim istoc nil est magis etc.,: At enim vereor, inquit Crassus, ne haec etc.,: cum dixisset Sophocles, O puerum pulchrum, Pericle. At enim praetorem, Sophocle, decet non solum manus, sed etiam oculos abstinentes habere, etc., Beier; so ; : at enim inter hos ipsos existunt graves controversiae,; so ; ; ; : At enim cur a me potissimum hoc praesidium petiverunt?: At enim quis reprehendet, quod in parricidas rei publicae decretum erit? Kritz: At enim quid ita solus ego circum curam ago?; : At enim eo foedere, quod etc.,; ; : At enim nova nobis in fratrum filias conjugia; sed etc.,.—
By tamen: Jam id peccatum primum magnum, magnum, at humanum tamen, : Hi secretis sermonibus ... conveniunt; nam publice civitas talibus inceptis abhorrebat. At tamen interfuere quidam etc.,: At certe tamen, inquiunt, quod etc.,.—
With a preced. negative, sometimes no antithesis is appended by at, but it is indicated that if what has been said is not true, yet at least something else is true, but yet; sometimes with tamen, but yet; or certe, but at least, yet at least: Nolo victumas: at minimis me extis placare volo,: Si tibi non cordi fuerant conubia nostra, ... At tamen in vostras potuisti ducere sedes,: Non cognoscebantur foris, at domi: non ab alienis, at a suis,: Liceat haec nobis, si oblivisci non possumus, at tacere,: Si genus humanum et mortalia temnitis arma, At sperate deos memores fandi atque nefandi,; so , and 6, 406. —With certe: Haec erant ... quorum cognitio studiosis juvenibus si non magnam utilitatem adferet, at certe, quod magis petimus, bonam voluntatem,; ; , al.—
The antithesis is sometimes not so much in the clause appended by at, as in the persons or things introduced in it; so,
Esp. freq. in conditional clauses with si, si non, si minus, etiam si, etc.; cf. Herm. ad Viger. 241: Si ego hic peribo, ast ille, ut dixit, non redit; At erit mi hoc factum mortuo memorabile, if I perish here, but he does not return, yet etc., ; : si ego digna hac contumeliā Sum maxime, at tu indignus qui faceres tamen,: Si tu oblitus es, at di meminerunt,: si non eo die, at postridie,: si non paulo, at aliquanto (post petīsses),; ; : quanta tempestas invidiae nobis, si minus in praesens, at in posteritatem impendeat,; ; : qui non possit, etiam si sine ullā suspitione, at non sine argumento male dicere, .—
With etsi: ei, etsi nequāquam parem illius ingenio, at pro nostro tamen studio meritam gratiam referamus,; .—
With quod si: Quod si nihil cum potentiore juris humani relinquitur inopi, at ego ad deos confugiam,; .—
At, like autem and δέ, sometimes serves simply to introduce an explanation: cum Sic mutilus miniteris. At illi foeda cicatrix etc., now an ugly scar etc., . —
And also like δέ in Hom. and Hdt., it sometimes introduces an apodosis,
With si: Bellona, si hobie nobis victoriam duis, ast ego templum tibi voveo, if to-day thou bestow victory, then I etc., ἐάν—δέ, .—
With quoniam: Nunc, quoniam tuum insanabile ingenium est, at tu tuo supplicio doce etc., since your disposition is past cure, at least etc., ἐπεί—δέ, .!*?
At is sometimes repeated at the beginning of several clauses,
In opposition each to the preceding clause: Soph. Tu quidem haut etiam octoginta's pondo. Paegn. At confidentiā Militia illa militatur multo magis quam pondere. At ego hanc operam perdo, : Si ego hic peribo, ast ille, ut dixit, non redit: At erit mi hoc factum mortuo memorabile,; sqq. (Cic., in Quir. 7 and 10, opposes at to sed, and Tac., in A. 12, 6, sed to at).—
In opposition to some common clause preceding: At etiam asto? At etiam cesso foribus facere hisce assulas?: Quid tum esse existimas judicatum? Certe gratīs judicāsse. At condemnārat; at causam totam non audierat; at in contionibus etc.,: Sit flagitiorum omnium princeps: at est bonus imperator, at felix,; ; B. and K.: Nefarius Hippias Pisistrati filius arma contra patriam ferens; at Sulla, at Marius, at Cinna recte, imo jure fortasse,: At non formosa est, at non bene culta puella; At, puto, non votis saepe petita meis? Merk.: At quam sunt similes, at quam formosus uterque!: rideri possit eo quod Rusticius tonso toga defluit: at est bonus ut melior vir Non alius quisquam; at tibi amicus; at ingenium ingens Inculto latet hoc sub corpore, sqq. (cf. sed— sed,; ; ; and a similar use of ἀλλά in Hellenistic Greek, as ἀλλά—ἀλλά, 2 Cor. 2, 17: ἀλλά—ἀλλά —ἀλλά, 1 Cor. 6, 11).—
Though regularly occupying the first place in its clause or sentence, it sometimes stands second (cf. atque fin.): Saepius at si me, Lycida formose, revisas,; : Tutior at quanto merx est in classe secundā,: Mentior at si quid, etc.,: Gramineis ast inde toris discumbitur,: Major at inde etc.,.—See more upon this word in Hand, Turs. I. pp. 417-451; Wagner, Quaest. XXXVII. ad Verg. IV. pp. 581- 585.

la:conj:atque.html:
atque or āc (atque is used before vowels and consonants, ac, in class. lang., only before consonants;
v.infra, I.), conj. [at has regularly in the compound atque a continuative, as in atqui it has an adversative force; pr. and further, and besides, and also; cf. in Gr. πρὸς δέ, πρὸς δὲ ἔτι, ἔτι καί, ἔτι δέ, and τὲ καί; v. at init., and for the change of form atque, ac, cf. neque, nec; in MSS. and inscriptions sometimes written adque, and sometimes by confusion at-qui], a copulative particle, and also, and besides, and even, and (indicating a close internal connection between single words or whole clauses; while et designates an external connection of diff. objects with each other, v. et; syn.: et, -que, autem, praeterea, porro, ad hoc, ad haec).
In joining single words, which is its most common use.
In gen. (The following representation is based on a collection of all the instances of the use of atque and ac in , Phil. 2, Tusc. 1, and Off. 1; in and 2; in ; and in ; and wherever in the account either author or work is not cited, there atque or ac does not occur.)
The form atque.
Before vowels and h.—Before a (very freq.): sociorum atque amicorum,; ; ; ; ; ; ; 2, 14; ; ; ; .—Before e (very freq.): deposci atque expeti,; ; ; id. Phil, 2, 21, 51; 2, 21, 52; ; ; ; ; 2, 19; ; ; ; .—Before i (very freq.): excitare atque inflammare,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 2, 1 bis; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before o (freq. in Cic.): honestissimus atque ornatissimus,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before u (very rare), ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before h (not infreq.): Sertorianae atque Hispaniensis,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Before consonants.—Before b (very rare): Gallorum atque Belgarum,; so, Cassius atque Brutus,.—Before c (infreq. in Cic., freq. in Sall.): in portubus atque custodiis,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 26, 4; 29, 3.—Before d (infreq.): superatam esse atque depressam,; : ; ; ; ; ; .—Before f (infreq.): vitiis atque flagitiis,; ; ; ; ; ; .— Before g (very rare): dignitate atque gloria,; : virtute atque gloria,; .—Before j (very rare): labore atque justitia,; .—Before l (rare): hilari atque laeto,; ; ; ; .—Before m (infreq. in Cic., once in Caes.): multae atque magnae,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 51, 1.—Before n (infreq.): adventu atque nomine,; ; ; bis.—Before p (infreq. in Cic.): magna atque praeclara,; ; ; ; ; ; ; 20, 3.—Before q (does not occur).—Before r (rare): se conlegit atque recreavit,.— Before s (rare in Cic.): provinciarum atque sociorum,; ; ; ; ; .— Before t (infreq.): parietum atque tectorum,; ; ; ; ; .—Before v (infreq.): gravis atque vehemens,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
The form ac before consonants.—Before b (very rare): sentientes ac bene meritos,: feri ac barbari, and 33.—Before c (very rare): liberis ac conjugibus,: Romae ac circa urbem,.—Before d (freq. in Cic.): periculum ac discrimen,; ; ; ; ; : usus ac disciplina,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before f (infreq.): opima est ac fertilis,; ; ; ; : potentissimos ac firmissimos,; ; ; 2, 13: pessuma ac flagitiosissima,; ; .—Before g (does not occur).—Before j (very rare): nobilitatis ac juventutis,.—Before l (not infreq. in Liv.), ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before m (not infreq. in Cic.): terrore ac metu,; bis; 20, 59; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before n (not infreq. in Cic.): insedit ac nimis inveteravit,: gentes ac nationes,; 12, 35 bis; ; ; ; ; .—Before p (not infreq. in Cic., Caes., and Liv.): celeberrimum ac plenissimum,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 2, 19; ; ; ; .—Before q (does not occur).—Before r (infreq.): firmamenti ac roboris,; ; ; ; ; ; .—Before s (freq. in Cic. and Liv., infreq. in Caes.): vectigalibus ac sociis,; ; ; ; ; ; ; 2, 24; ; bis; 21, 36.—Before t (infreq. in Cic., freq. in Liv.): tantis rebus ac tanto bello,bis; 19, 56; 20, 59; ; ; ; ter; 21, 10; 21, 14; 21, 25.—Before v (not in Cic., only once in Caes. and Sall., but freq. in Liv.): armatos ac victores,: inconsulte ac veluti etc.,: opera ac vineae,; ; ; 21, 43. —(So in the phrases treated below: atque adeo, atque alter or alius, atque eccum, atque eo, atque etiam, atque illuc, atque is or hic, atque iterum, atque omnia, atque ut, atque late, atque sic, atque velut, but ac ne, ac si, and ac tamen).—With simul: Britannorum acies in speciem simul ac terrorem editioribus locis constiterat,: in se simul atque in Herculem,: suos prosequitur simul ac deponit,; so, sociis pariter atque hostibus,: innocentes ac noxios juxta cadere,.—Hence, sometimes syn. with et—et, ut—ita, aeque ac; both—and, as—so, as well—as, as well as: hodie sero ac nequiquam

voles, (cf. : verum et sero et nequidquam pudet): copia sententiarum atque verborum,: omnia honesta atque inhonesta,: nobiles atque ignobiles,: caloris ac frigoris patientia par,; ; : vir bonus et prudens dici delector ego ac tu,.—

Esp.
In a hendiadys: utinam isto animo atque virtute in summā re publicā versari quam in municipali maluisset,with this virtuous feeling,: de conplexu ejus ac sinu,of his bosom embrace,: me eadem, quae ceteros, fama atque invidia vexabat, i. e. invidiosa fama,: clamore atque adsensu,shout of applause,.—
In joining to the idea of a preceding word one more important, and indeed, and even, and especially (v. Kritz ad ).
Absol.: Pa. Nempe tu istic ais esse erilem concubinam? Sc. Atque arguo me etc., yea and I maintain that I etc., : Ph. Tun vidisti? Sc. Atque his quidem oculis, : Ps. Ecquid habet is homo aceti in pectore? Ch. Atque acidissimi, ; so ; : Py. Cognoscitne (ea)? Ch. Ac memoriter, : Faciam boni tibi aliquid pro istā re ac lubens,and with a good will,: rem difficilem (dii immortales) atque omnium difficillimam,and indeed,: magna diis immortalibus habenda est gratia atque huic ipsi Jovi Statori, etc.,and especially,: hebeti ingenio atque nullo,and in fact,: ex plurimis periculis et insidiis atque ex mediā morte,and even,: fratre meo atque eodem propinquo suo interfecto,and at the same time,: intra moenia atque in sinu urbis,.—
With adeo, and that too, and even: intra moenia atque adeo in senatu,: qui in urbe remanserunt atque adeo qui contra urbis salutem etc.,: insto atque urgeo, insector, posco atque adeo flagito crimen,: non petentem atque adeo etiam absentem,.—And with autem also added: atque adeo autem quor etc.,.—
With etiam: id jam populare atque etiam plausibile factum est,and also,: ne Verginio commeatum dent atque etiam in custodiā habeant,.—
With the dem. pron. hic, is: negotium magnum est navigare atque id mense Quintili,and besides, and that, and that too,; : maximis defixis trabibus atque eis praeacutis,: Asseres pedum XII. cuspidibus praefixis atque hi maximis ballistis missi,: duabus missis subsidio cohortibus a Caesare, atque his primis legionum duarum,; : flumen uno omnino loco pedibus atque hoc aegre transiri potest,: ad celeritatem onerandi subductionesque paulo facit humiliores ... atque id eo magis, quod, etc.,; cf. without id (perh. to avoid the repetition of the pron.): quā (sc. virtute) nostri milites facile superabant, atque eo magis, quod, etc., and that the more because etc., fin.: dicendi artem aptā trepidatione occultans atque eo validior,; ; ; .—
In comparisons.
Of equality (Rudd. II. p. 94; Zumpt, § 340); with par, idem, item, aequus, similis, juxta, talis, totidem, etc., as: et nota, quod ex hujus modi structurā Graecā (sc. ὅμοιος καί, etc.) frequenter Latini ac et atque in significatione similitudinis accipiunt, Prisc. pp. 1192 and 1193 P.; cf. ; Lidd. and Scott, s. v. καί, III.: si parem sententiam hic habet ac formam,: quom opulenti loquuntur pariter atque ignobiles, Enn. ap. : Ecastor pariter hoc atque alias res soles,: pariter nunc operā me adjuves ac re dudum opitulata es,: neque enim mihi par ratio cum Lucilio est ac tecum fuit,: parique eum atque illos imperio esse jussit,: magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio fugavit,: pariter patribus ac plebi carus,: nam et vita est eadem et animus te erga idem ac fuit, Ter. Heaut. 2, 3, 24: In hanc argumentationes ex eisdem locis sumendae sunt atque in causam negotialem,: equi quod alii sunt ad rem militarem idonei, alii ad vecturam ... non item sunt spectandi atque habendi,; Müll.: cum ex provinciā populi Romani aequam partem tu tibi sumpseris atque populo Romano miseris,: Modo ne in aequo (jure) hostes apud vos sint ac nos socii, (exs. with aeque; v. aeque, δ); : et simili jure tu ulcisceris patrui mortem atque ille persequeretur fratris sui, si, etc.,; ; : similem pavorem inde ac fugam fore, ac bello Gallico fuerit,; : contendant, se juxta hieme atque aestate bella gerere posse,; cf. Drak. ad : faxo eum tali mactatum, atque hic est, infortunio,; : cum totidem navibus atque erat profectus,.—
Of difference; with alius and its derivv., with dissimile, contra, contrarius, secus, etc., than: illi sunt alio ingenio atque tu,other than, different from,; v. the passages under alius, I. B. α: aliter tuum amorem atque est accipis,; v. the passages under aliter, 1. a.; cf. also aliorsum, II., and aliusmodi: quod est non dissimile atque ire in Solonium,: simulacrum in excelso collocare et, contra atque ante fuerat, ad orientem convertere,: vides, omnia fere contra ac dicta sint evenisse,; : qui versantur retro, contrario motu atque caelum,: membra paulo secus a me atque ab illo partita,: cujus ego salutem non secus ac meam tueri debeo, al.; v. contra, contrarius, secus, etc.—
Sometimes, in cases of equality or difference, atque with ut or ac with si (with aliter affirm. Cic. appears to connect only atque ut, not ac si; once, however, non aliter, ac si,; v. aliter, 1. b.): pariter hoc fit atque ut alia facta sunt,: nec fallaciam Astutiorem ullus fecit poëta atque Ut haec est fabre facta a nobis, sqq.: quod iste aliter atque ut edixerat decrevisset,: et qui suos casus aliter ferunt atque ut auctores aliis ipsi fuerunt, etc.,: si mentionem fecerint, quo aliter ager possideretur atque ut ex legibus Juliis,; , c; cf. Wopk. Lect. Tull. 1, 15, p. 118; : Egnatii absentis rem ut tueare, aeque a te peto ac si mea negotia essent,just as if,: tu autem similiter facis ac si me roges, etc.,: reliquis officiis, juxta ac si meus frater esset, sustentavit,: quod dandum est amicitiae, large dabitur a me non secus ac si meus esset frater,: haec sunt, tribuni, consilia vestra, non, hercule, dissimilia, ac si quis, etc., al. —
More rare with nimis, in partem, pro eo, etc.; in Plaut. also with mutare or demutare = aliud esse: nimis bellus, atque ut esse maxume optabam, locus,: haud centensumam Partem dixi atque, otium rei si sit, possim expromere,: sane quam pro eo ac debui graviter molesteque tuli, just as was my duty, Sulp. ap. : debeo sperare, omnes deos, qui huic urbi praesident, pro eo mihi, ac mereor, relaturos gratiam esse,: pro eo, ac si concessum sit, concludere oportebit argumentationem,: non possum ego non aut proxime atque ille aut etiam aeque laborare,nearly the same as he,: neque se luna quoquam mutat atque uti exorta est semel,: num quid videtur demutare atque ut quidem Dixi?.—
Sometimes the word indicating comparison (aeque, tantopere, etc.) is to be supplied from the connection (in the class. per. perh. used only once by Cassius in epist. style): nebula haud est mollis atque hujus est,: quem esse amicum ratus sum atque ipsus sum mihi,: quae suco caret atque putris pumex, (Müll., est putusque): digne ac mereor commendatus esse, Cass. ap. ; ; , 2, 54.—
Poet. or in post-Aug. prose with comparatives (for quam), than: amicior mihi nullus vivit atque is est,: non Apollinis magis verum atque hoc responsum est, Ruhnk.: Illi non minus ac tibi Pectore uritur intimo Flamma,: haud minus ac jussi faciunt,: Non tuus hoc capiet venter plus ac meus, Bentl. and Heind. (cf. infra: nihilo plus accipias quam Qui nil portārit): qui peccas minus atque ego,: Artius atque hedera procera adstringitur ilex,; Ruhnk. —
In the comparison of two periods of time, most freq. with simul (v. examples under simul); ante- or post-class. with principio, statim: principio Atque animus ephebis aetate exiit,as soon as,: judici enim, statim atque factus est, omnium rerum officium incumbit,: quamvis, statim atque intercessit, mulier competierat,.—
To connect a negative clause which explains or corrects what precedes; hence sometimes with potius (class.; in Cic. very freq., but rare in the poets), and not, and not rather.
Absol.: Decipiam ac non veniam,: si fidem habeat, ... ac non id metuat, ne etc.,: perparvam vero controversiam dicis, ac non eam, quae dirimat omnia,: quasi nunc id agatur, quis ex tantā multitudine occiderit, ac non hoc quaeratur, eum, etc.,: si (mundum) tuum ac non deorum immortalium domicilium putes, nonne plane desipere videare?: nemo erat, qui illum reum ac non miliens condemnatum arbitraretur,: si hoc dissuadere est, ac non disturbare ac pervertere,: si res verba desideraret ac non pro se ipsa loqueretur,: hoc te exspectare tempus tibi turpe est ac non ei rei sapientiā tuā te occurrere, Serv. ap. : velut destituti ac non qui ipsi destituissent,; fin.: si mihi mea sententia proferenda ac non disertissimorum,.—
With potius: Quam ob rem scriba deducet, ac non potius mulio, qui advexit? (B. and K., et): quis (eum) ita aspexit, ut perditum civem, ac non potius ut importunissimum hostem?.— Pliny the elder commonly employs in this sense atque non, not ac non: concremāsse ea (scrinia) optumā fide atque non legisse,; ; ; 27, 9, 55, § 78; 31, 7, 39, § 73 et saep. —
In connecting clauses and beginning periods.
In gen., and, and so, and even, and too: Pamph. Antiquam adeo tuam venustatem obtines. Bacch. Ac tu ecastor morem antiquom atque ingenium obtines, And you too, : atque illi (philosopho) ordiri placet etc.,: Africanus indigens mei? Minime hercle. Ac ne ego quidem illius, And I indeed not, etc., ; : cum versus facias, te ipsum percontor, etc. ... Atque ego cum Graecos facerem, natus mare citra, Versiculos, etc.,: multa quippe et diversa angebant: validior per Germaniam exercitus, etc. ... quos igitur anteferret? ac (i. e. similiter angebat), ne postpositi contumeliā incenderentur,: Minime, minime, inquit Secundus, atque adeo vellem maturius intervenisses,: ac similiter in translatione, etc.,.—
In adducing new arguments of similar force in favor of any assertion or making further statements about a subject, etc.; cf. Beier ad .
Absol.: maxima est enim vis vetustatis et consuetudinis: atque in ipso equo, cujus modo mentionem feci, si, etc.,and furthermore, and moreover,: Atque, si natura confirmatura jus non erit, virtutes omnes tollentur, B. and K. —
Often with etiam: Atque alias etiam dicendi virtutes sequitur,: Atque hoc etiam animadvertendum non esse omnia etc.,; so ; ; .—
Sometimes with quoque: Atque occidi quoque Potius quam cibum praehiberem,; so ; , and ; .—
And even with quoque etiam: Atque ego

quoque etiam, qui Jovis sum filius, Contagione etc., .—

In narration: aegre submoventes obvios intrare portam, qui adducebant Philopoemenem, potuerunt: atque conferta turba iter reliquum clauserat,; fin.: completur caede, quantum inter castra murosque vacui fuit: ac rursus nova laborum facies,; cf. and 2, 29 init.—
In introducing comparisons, atque ut, atque velut (mostly poet., esp. in epic poetry): Atque ut perspicio, profecto etc.,: ac veluti magno in populo cum saepe coörta est Seditio.... Sic cunctus pelagi cecidit fragor, etc.,; so ; ; ; ; 6, 707; 9, 59; 10, 405; 10, 707; 10, 803; 11, 809; 12, 365; 12, 521; 12, 684; 12, 715; 12, 908: Inclinare meridiem Sentis ac, veluti stet volucris dies, Parcis deripere etc.,; ; and so, Ac velut in nigro jactatis turbine nautis, etc. ... Tale fuit nobis Manius auxilium, (for which Sillig and Müller read: Hic velut, etc.): Atque ut magnas utilitates adipiscimur, etc.,: Atque ut hujus mores veros amicos parere non potuerunt, sic etc.,.—
In connecting two acts or events.
In the order of time, and then; hence the ancient grammarians assume in it the notion of quick succession, and explain it, though improperly, as syn. with statim, ilico, without any accompanying copulative, v. ; (only in the poets and histt.): Atque atque accedit muros Romana juventus (the repetition of the atque represents the approach step by step), Enn. ap. Gell. and Non. l. l. (Ann. v. 527 Müll.): Quo imus unā; ad prandium? Atque illi tacent,And then they are silent,: Ubi cenamus? inquam, atque illi abnuunt,and upon this they shake their head,; : dum circumspecto atque ego lembum conspicor,; so ; ; : lucernam forte oblitus fueram exstinguere: Atque ille exclamat derepente maximum,and then he suddenly exclaims,: cui fidus Achates It comes ... atque illi Misenum in litore sicco Ut venere, vident, etc., and as they thus came, etc., : dixerat, atque illi sese deus obtulit ultro,; ; ; : tum Otho ingredi castra ausus: atque illum tribuni centurionesque circumsistunt,. —Sometimes with two imperatives, in order to indicate vividly the necessity of a quicker succession, or the close connection between two actions: cape hoc argentum atque defer,: abi domum ac deos comprecare,: tace modo ac sequere hac,: Accipe carmina atque hanc sine tempora circum hederam tibi serpere,; ; ; : Da auxilium, pater, atque haec omina firma,; ; ; 3, 639; 4, 424; 9, 90; 10, 624; 11, 370.—
In the order of thought, and so, and thus, and therefore.
Absol.: si nunc de tuo jure concessisses paululum, Atque adulescenti morigerāsses,and so,.—
With ita or sic: Ventum deinde ad multo angustiorem rupem, atque ita rectis saxis, etc.,; : ac sic prope innumerabiles species reperiuntur,.—
Connecting conclusion and condition, so, then (cf. at, II. F.): non aliter quam qui adverso vix flumine lembum Remigiis subigit, si bracchia forte remisit, Atque illum praeceps prono rapit alveus amni, (here explained by statim by , and by Servius, but thus its connective force is wholly lost; cf. also Forbig ad h. l. for still another explanation).—
(As supra, I. c.) To annex a thought of more importance: Satisne videtur declarāsse Dionysius nihil esse ei beatum, cui semper aliqui terror impendeat? atque ei ne integrum quidem erat, ut ad justitiam remigraret,; : hoc enim spectant leges, hoc volunt, incolumem esse civium conjunctionem, quam qui dirimunt, eos morte ... coërcent. Atque hoc multo magis efficit ipsa naturae ratio,; : hac spe lapsus Induciomarus ... exsules damnatosque totā Galliā magnis praemiis ad se allicere coepit; ac tantam sibi jam iis rebus in Galliā auctoritatem comparaverat, ut, etc.,; ; .—Hence also in answers, in order to confirm a question or assertion: Sed videone ego Pamphilippum cum fratre Epignomo? Atque is est,And he it is, Yes, it is he,; so : Th. Mihin malum minitare? Ca. Atque edepol non minitabor, sed dabo, : Ch. Egon formidulosus? nemost hominum, qui vivat, minus. Th. Atque ita opust, .—
In expressing a wish, atque utinam: Veritus sum arbitros, atque utinam memet possim obliscier! Att., Trag. Rel. p. 160 Rib.: videmus enim fuisse quosdam, qui īdem ornate ac graviter, īdem versute et subtiliter dicerent. Atque utinam in Latinis talis oratoris simulacrum reperire possemus!; so : Atque utinam pro decore etc.,: Atque utinam ex vobis unus etc.,; : Atque utinam ... Ille vir in medio fiat amore lapis!; ; ; 3, 8, 19 al.—
To connect an adversative clause, and often fully with tamen, and yet, notwithstanding, nevertheless.
Absol.: Mihi quidem hercle non fit veri simile; atque ipsis commentum placet, Ruhnk. (atque pro tamen, Don.): ego quia non rediit filius, quae cogito! ... Atque ex me hic natus non est, sed ex fratre, (Quasi dicat, ex me non est, et sic afficior: quid paterer si genuissem? Don.; cf. Acron. ap. P.); Beier; Matth.: ceterum ex aliis negotiis, quae ingenio exercentur, in primis magno usui est memoria rerum gestarum ... Atque ego credo fore qui, etc.,and yet I believe, and 3 Corte; : observare principis egressum in publicum, insidere vias examina infantium futurusque populus solebat. Labor parentibus erat ostentare parvulos ... Ac plerique insitis precibus surdas principis aures obstrepebant,.—
With tamen: nihil praeterea est magnopere dicendum. Ac tamen, ne cui loco non videatur esse responsum, etc.,: discipulos dissimilīs inter se ac tamen laudandos,; : Atque in his tamen tribus generibus etc.,; ; ; ; fin. (cf. in reference to the last four passages Wund. Varr. Lectt. p. lviii. sq.): ac tamen initia fastigii etc.,; ; ; 14, 21: pauciores cum pluribus certāsse, ac tamen fusos Germanos,.—
To connect a minor affirmative proposition (the assumptio or propositio minor of logical lang.) in syllogisms, now, but, but now (while atqui is used to connect either an affirmative or negative minor premiss: v. atqui): Scaptius quaternas postulabat. Metui, si impetrāsset, ne tu ipse me amare desineres; ... Atque hoc tempore ipso impingit mihi epistulam etc.,.—Sometimes the conclusion is to be supplied: nisi qui naturas hominum, penitus perspexerit, dicendo, quod volet, perficere non poterit. Atque totus hic locus philosophorum putatur proprius (conclusion: ergo oratorem philosophiam cognoscere oportet), and 54.—
In introducing a purpose (freq. in Cic.).
A negative purpose, and esp. in anticipating an objection: Ac ne sine causā videretur edixisse,: Ac ne forte hoc magnum ac mirabile esse videatur,; so : Ac ne saepius dicendum sit,: Ac ne forte roges, quo me duce, quo lare tuter,: Ac ne forte putes,: Ac ne forte putes etc., (Merkel, Et).—
A positive purpose: Atque ut ejus diversa studia in dissimili ratione perspicere possitis, nemo etc.,: Atque ut omnes intellegant me etc. ... dico etc.,; ; ; ; : Atque ut C. Flaminium relinquam etc.,; .—
In continuing a thought in assertions or narration, and, now, and now, : audistis, cum pro se diceret, genus orationis, etc., ... perspexistis. Atque in eo non solum ingenium ejus videbatis, etc., ; so ; ; ; ; ; , Bremi; ; ; ; : ac si, sublato illo, depelli a vobis omne periculum judicarem, now if I, etc., : atque si etiam hoc natura praescribit, etc.,; so ; .—
In introducing parentheses: vulgo credere, Penino (atque inde nomen et jugo Alpium inditum) transgressum,: omne adfectūs genus (atque ea maxime jucundam et ornatam faciunt orationem) de luxuriā, etc., MSS., where Halm after Spalding reads et quae.—
At the conclusion of a discourse (not infreq. in Cic.): Atque in primis duabus dicendi partibus qualis esset, summatim breviterque descripsimus, And thus have we, then, briefly described, etc., : Ac de primo quidem officii fonte diximus,: Ac de inferendā quidem injuriā satis dictum est,; —
In particular connections and phrases.
Unus atque alter, one and the other; alius atque alius, one and another; now this, now that: unae atque alterae scalae,: quarum (coclearum) cum unam atque alteram, dein plures peteret,: unum atque alterum lacum integer perfluit,: dilatisque aliā atque aliā de causā comitiis,; : alius atque alius,; (v. alius, II. D.).—Also separated by several words: aliud ejus subinde atque aliud facientes initium,.—
Etiam atque etiam. again and again: temo Stellas cogens etiam atque etiam Noctis sublime iter, Enn., Trag. Rel. p. 39 Rib.: etiam atque etiam cogita,: etiam atque etiam considera,: monitos eos etiam atque etiam volo,.—So, semel atque iterum, ; ; ; and: iterum atque iterum,; .—
Huc atque illuc, hither and thither, ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Longe atque late, far and wide, : atque eccum or atque eccum video, in colloquial lang.: Heus vocate huc Davom. Atque eccum,but here he is,: Audire vocem visa sum modo militis. Atque eccum,and here he is,; so .—
Atque omnia, in making an assertion general, and so generally: Atque in eis omnibus, quae sunt actionis, inest quaedam vis a naturā data,: quorum (verborum) descriptus ordo alias aliā terminatione concluditur, atque omnia illa et prima et media verba spectare debent ad ultimum,; : commoda civium non divellere, atque omnes aequitate eādem continere, and so rather, etc., : nihil acerbum esse, nihil crudele, atque omnia plena clementiae, humanitatis,: Atque omnis vitae ratio sic constat, ut, quae probamus in aliis, facere ipsi velimus,.—
With other conjunctions.
After et: equidem putabam virtutem hominibus instituendo et persuadendo, non minis et vi ac metu tradi,: Magnifica vero vox et magno viro ac sapiente digna,; : vanus aspectus et auri fulgor atque argenti,.: denuntiarent, ut ab Saguntinis abstineret et Carthaginem in Africam traicerent ac sociorum querimonias deferrent,: ubi et fratrem consilii ac periculi socium haberem,: et uti liter demum ac Latine perspicueque,: Nam et subtili plenius aliquid atque subtilius et vehementi remissius atque vehementius invenitur,. —
After que, as in Gr. τὲ καί: litterisque ac laudibus aeternare, Varr. ap. : submoverique atque in castra redigi,: terrorem caedemque ac fugam fecere,: mus Sub terris posuitque domos atque horrea fecit,; ; .—
Before et: caelum ipsum ac mare et silvas circum spectantes,.—
After neque (only in the poets and post - Aug. prose): nec clavis nec canis atque calix,: naturam Oceani atque aestūs

neque quaerere hujus operis est, ac multi retulere, : mediocritatem pristinam neque dissimulavit umquam ac frequenter etiam prae se tulit,.—

Atque repeated, esp. in arch. Lat.: Scio solere plerisque hominibus in rebus secundis atque prolixis atque prosperis animum excellere atque superbiam atque ferociam augescere atque crescere, Cato ap. : Dicere possum quibus villae atque aedes aedificatae atque expolitae maximo opere citro atque ebore atque pavimentis Poenicis stent, Cato ap. Müll.: atque ut C. Flamininum atque ea, quae jam prisca videntur, propter vetustatem relinquam,: omnem dignitatem tuam in virtute atque in rebus gestis atque in tuā gravitate positam existimare,.—Esp. freq. in enumerations in the poets: Haec atque illa dies atque alia atque alia,: Mavortia tellus Atque Getae atque Hebrus,: Clioque et Beroë atque Ephyre Atque Opis et Asia,.—And sometimes forming a double connective, both— and = et—et: Multus ut in terras deplueretque lapis: Atque tubas atque arma ferunt crepitantia caelo Audita,: complexa sui corpus miserabile nati Atque deos atque astra vocat crudelia mater,; ; v. Forbig ad Verg. l. l.!*? Atque regularly stands at the beginning of its sentence or clause or before the word it connects, but in poetry it sometimes, like et and at, stands:
In the second place: Jamque novum terrae stupeant lucescere solem, Altius atque cadant imbres, Rib., ubi v. Forbig.: Accipite ergo animis atque haec mea figite dicta,, and 10, 104 (animis may, however, here be taken with Accipite, as in ): Esto beata, funus atque imagines Ducant triumphales tuum,; ; ; (ubi v. Fritzsche).—
In the third place: quod pubes hederā virente Gaudeant pullā magis atque myrto,; cf. at fin. (Vid. more upon this word in Hand, Turs. I. pp. 452-513.)

A surname of T. Pomponius, the intimate friend of Cicero, given to him on account of his long residence at Athens. His biography is found in Nepos.—
A friend of Ovid, ; . —

at-trĭbŭo (adt-, Weissenb., Jan; att-, B. and K., L. Müller), ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.,

Esp.

T. t., to lay as a tax or tribute: his rebus omnibus terni in milia aeris adtribuerentur,.—Hence, attrĭbūtus (adt-), a, um, P. a., lit. that is ascribed or attributed to a thing; hence, subst.: attrĭbūtum, i, n.

la:conj:atqui.html:
at-qui (in MSS. sometimes adqui, e. g. Mai, and often confounded with atque),
conj. (the form atquin is incorrect and post-class.; for , should be read at quin separately, Fleck.; cf. Caper Orth. p. 2441) [qui, abl. of indef. quis, used adverbially; so pr. but anyhow; cf.: alioqui, ceteroqui].
In gen., serving to connect-an adversative clause or assertion, but anyhow, but any way or wise, yet, notwithstanding, however, rather, but now, but nevertheless, and yet, ἀλλὰ δή, ἀλλὰ δήπου, ἀλλὰ μήν (a purely adversative particle, a more emphatic at, while atque is regularly copulative; v. atque; syn.: at, sed, verum, autem; comparatively rare in all periods, it being scarcely more than an emphasized form of at): Th. Quid aïs, venefica? Py. Atqui certo comperi, : Sy. Gratiam habeo. De. Atqui, Syre, Hoc verumst et re ipsā experiere propediem, : Cl. Satis scite promittit tibi. Sy. Atqui tu hanc jocari credis? but yet do you believe that she is jesting? : cum omnia vi et armis egeris, accuses eum, qui se praesidio munierit, non ut te oppugnaret, sed ut vitam suam posset defendere? Atqui ne ex eo quidem tempore id egit Sestius, ut, etc.,and yet,: tum, ut me Cotta vidit, peropportune, inquit, venis ... atqui mihi quoque videor, inquam, venisse, ut dicis, opportune, rather I seem to myself, etc., ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ ἐμοὶ δοκῶ, : vitas hinnuleo me similis Chloe ... atqui non ego te tigris ut aspera Gaetulusve leo, frangere persequor, but yet, ἀλλά τοι, -10: Jam vero videtis nihil esse tam morti simile quam somnum; atqui dormientium animi maxime declarant divinitatem suam,but yet,: tum dixisse (Lysandrum), mirari se non modo diligentiam, sed etiam sollertiam ejus, a quo essent illa dimensa atque descripta: et ei Cyrum respondisse: Atqui (sc. ne putes alium id fecisse) ego omnia ista sum dimensus,.—
Esp.
In adding a thought confirmatory of a preceding one, but not antithetical (v. at init.), but indeed, but certainly, by all means: Do. Salvos sis, adulescens Sa. Siquidem hanc vendidero pretio suo. To. Atqui aut hoc emptore vendes pulcre aut alio non potest, : Et Philus: praeclaram vero causam ad me defertis, cum me improbitatis patrocinium suscipere vultis. Atqui id tibi, inquit Laelius, verendum est, but certainly (ironically), ; .—Sometimes with pol or sic: atqui pol hodie non feres, ni genua confricantur,: Py. Scis eam civem hinc esse? Pa. Nescio. Py. Atqui sic inventast, : hunc ego non diligam? non admirer? non omni ratione defendendum putem? Atqui sic a summis hominibus eruditissimis accepimus, etc., yet so we have certainly heard, etc., .—
So also atqui si, adversative, but if, or continuative, if now, if indeed (cf.: quod si): sine veniat. Atqui si illam digito attigerit, oculi illi ilico ecfodientur,if, however, he do but touch her, (Fleck., Qui): quae et conscripta a multis sunt diligenter et sunt humiliora quam illa, quae a nobis exspectari puto. Att. Atqui si quaeris ego quid exspectem, etc., ; : atqui, si ita placet, inquit Antonius, trademus etiam,well now, if,: atqui Si noles sanus, curres hydropicus, but now if you are unwilling, etc., : atqui si tempus est ullum jure hominis necandi, quae multa sunt, certe illud est,but if now there is any time,—
To modify a preceding negation or negative interrogation, yet, still, instead of that, rather: Ni. Numquam auferes hinc aurum. Ch. Atqui jam dabis, but, : Non sum apud me. Se. Atqui opus est nunc quom maxime ut sis, : O rem, inquis, difficilem et inexplicabilem. Atqui explicanda est,nevertheless,; : magnum narras, vix credibile. Atqui Sic habet,but in fact, so it is,; : modum statuarum haberi nullum placet? Atqui habeatur necesse est,; ; ; ; .—
To connect a minor proposition in a syllogism (both an affirmative and a negative, while atque only connects an affirm. proposition), but, but now, now: Ergo cum sol igneus sit, quia nullus ignis sine pastu aliquo possit permanere, necesse est aut ei similis sit igni, quem ... aut ei, qui ... atqui hic noster ignis etc., and 41: qui fortis est, idem est fidens ... Qui autem est fidens, is profecto non extimescit ... Atqui in quem cadit aegritudo, in eundem timor ... Ita fit, ut fortitudini aegritudo repugnet,: (mors) aut plane neglegenda est ... aut etiam optanda, si, etc. Atqui tertium certe nihil inveniri potest. Quid igitur timeam si, etc.,; . (Vid. more upon this word in Hand, Turs. I. pp. 513-524.)

B. 2.—

In gen., black, dark, gloomy, sad, dismal, unfortunate, etc.: funus,: formido, [173], and ; so, Timor,: cupressus,: dies,; : mors,: fila trium sororum,: Esquiliae (as a burying-place),dismal,: seu mors atris circumvolat alis,: cura,; ; : lites,: comes,: serpens,; : genius .. vultu mutabilis, albus et ater,.—In Roman civil life, dies atri are the days on which the state experienced some calamity, unlucky days. (This designation is said to have arisen from the Roman custom of marking every unfortunate day in the calendar with coal); ; ; ; Fest. s. v. nonarum, p. 179 Müll.; id. s. v. religiosus, p. 278 Müll.; ; and 16; Afran. ap. : si atro die faxit insciens, probe factum esto,.—

Lit.: super limen pedes attollere,: signa,: pallium attollere, i. e. accingere (v. accingo), * : illum (regem) omnes apes ... saepe attollunt umeris,: Nec semel irrisus triviis attollere curat Fracto crure planum, to raise up the juggler, to help him up, * Schmid: parvumque attollite natum,lift up,: caput,: oculos humo,: Et contra magnum potes hos (oculos) attollere solem,: Sed non attollere contra Sustinet haec oculos,: Attollens Joseph oculos vidit etc.,: timidum lumen ad lumina,: vultus jacentes,: corpus ulnis,: manus ad caelum,: cornua e mari,: attollite portas, principes,; : mare ventis,; cf.: Euphratem attolli,swollen,: se in femur,raises himself on his thigh,: se in auras,: se recto trunco,: attollentem se ab gravi casu,: a terrā se attollentem,.— With middle signif.: e mediis hunc (sc. Atlantem) harenis in caelum attolli prodidere,: attollitur monte Pione,.—Of buildings, to raise, erect, build: immensam molem,: arcem,: attollitur opus in altitudinem XXXX. cubitis,: turres in centenos vicenos[que] attollebantur,.—Poet.: cum die stativorum campum alacritate discursu pulvere attolleres,; cf. .—
Trop., to raise, elevate, exalt, sustain; also, to enlarge, aggrandize, to render prominent or conspicuous, to extol (so esp. freq. in Tac.): Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus,: ultro implacabilis ardet Attollitque animos,: ad consulatūs spem attollere animos,: rectos ac vividos animos non ut alii contundis ac deprimis, sed foves et attollis,: Frangit et attollit vires in milite causa,: attollique suum laetis ad sidera nomen vocibus,: quanto Ciceronis studio Brutus Cassiusque attollerentur,were distinguished, Ruhnk. (cf. : animadverti dici jam a quibusdam exornari etiam nimium a me Brutum, nimium Cassium ornari); so, insignibus triumphi,; ; ; ; : res per similitudinem,: his (frons) contrahitur, attollitur (is drawn up or raised), demittitur, : belloque et armis rem publicam,: cuncta in majus attollens,: sua facta, suos casus,.— Form attolo, of doubtful meaning: Quis vetat qui ne attolat? Pac., Trag. Rel. p. 82 Rib.: Custodite istunc vos, ne vim qui attolat neve attigat, p. 105 (= auferre or afferre, Non.).

Rel. p. 141 Rib.: re atroci percitus,: res tam scelesta, tam atrox, tam nefaria credi non potest,: saevissimi domini atrocissima effigies,: Agrippina semper atrox,always gloomy,; : filia longo dolore atrox,wild,: hiems,severe,: nox,: tempestas,: flagrantis hora Caniculae,: atrocissimae litterae,: bellum magnum et atrox,: facinus,: non alia ante pugna atrocior,: periculum atrox,dreadful,; so, negotium,: imperium (Manlii),harsh,: odium,violent, et saep.—Of discourse, violent, bitter: tunc admiscere huic generi orationis vehementi atque atroci genus illud alterum ... lenitatis et mansuetudinis,: Summa concitandi adfectūs accusatori in hoc est, ut id, quod objecit, aut quam atrocissimum aut etiam quam maxime miserabile esse videatur,: peroratio,: et cuncta terrarum subacta Praeter atrocem animum Catonis,stern, unyielding,: fides (Reguli),; so, virtus,: ut verba atroci (i. e. rigido) stilo effoderent,.—Hence of that which is fixed, certain, invincible: occisa est haec res, nisi reperio atrocem mi aliquam astutiam, Lind. la:noun:atrium.html:
ātrĭum, ii, n.
acc. to Scaliger, from αἴθριον, subdiale, since it was a part of the uncovered portion of the house (but the atrium of the Romans was always covered); acc. to Müll., from the Tuscan town Atria, where this style of architecture originated; cf. Paul. ex Müll.; and Müller, Etrusk. 1, p. 254 sq.; but better from ater, acc. to the explanation of Servius: ibi etiam culina erat, unde et atrium dictum est; atrum enim erat ex fumo, ad
.
The fore-court, hall, entrance-room, entry; that part of the Roman house into which one first came after passing the entrance (janua); cf. ; O. Müller, Archaeol. III. § 293, and Etrusk. above cited. In earlier times, the atrium was used as a dining-room, Cato ap. . Here stood, opposite the door, the lectus genialis, ; here sat the housewife with her maidens spinning,; here clients were in attendance,; and 91; and here hung the family portraits and other paintings,; ; ; ; ; —Poet. in the plur., of a single atrium: Apparet domus intus et atria longa patescunt,; so ; —Meton. for the house itself: nec capient Phrygias atria nostra nurus,; .—So of the entrance-room in the dwelling of the gods: dextrā laevāque deorum Atria nobilium (as it were clients, v.supra) valvis celebrantur apertis, ; .—
In temples and other public buildings there was often an atrium, a hall, court: in atrio Libertatis,; ; ; ; : Vestae,; also called atrium regium,; cf. ; : atrium tabernaculi,; : in atriis Domūs Dei,; ; Smith, Dict. Antiq.—So atrium auctionarium,an auction-hall, auction-room,; so ; and absol., atria: cum desertis Aganippes Vallibus esuriens migraret in atria Clio,. Such halls were the Atria Licinia, : ATRIVM SVTORIVM, the shoemakers' hall, a place in Rome, Calend. Praenest. .

Atlas, a high mountain in Mauretania, in the northwest part of Libya, on which, acc. to the fable, heaven rested, sqq.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; (cf. Hom. Od. 1, 52; 4, 385; Hdt. 3, 2; 4, 148; Apollod. 2, 5, 11; Diod. Sic. 3, 5).—
In mythology, a king of Mauretania, son of Iapetus and Clymene, a lover of astronomy, ; ; changed by Perseus, with the aid of Medusa's head, into Mount Atlas, because he refused him a hospitable reception as guest, He was the father, by Pleione, of the seven Pleiades, and, by Æthra, of the seven (acc. to Hyg. five) Hyades.—Meton. for a man of colossal height, and iron. for a dwarf, .—

la:verb:attono.html:
at-tŏno (better than adt-), ŭi, ĭtum, 1, v. a.,
to thunder at; hence, to stun, stupefy (a poet. word of the Aug. per.; most frequent as P. a.; syn.: percello, perturbo, terreo): altitudo attonat, Maecen. ap. : quis furor vestras attonuit mentes!; .—Hence, attŏnĭtus (adt-), a, um, P. a., thundered at; hence trop. as in Gr. ἐμβροντηθείς, ἐμβρόντητος.
Thunderstruck, stunned, terrified, stupefied, astonished, amazed, confounded: attonitus est stupefactus. Nam proprie attonitus dicitur, cui casus vicini fulminis et sonitus tonitruum dant stuporem,: quo fragore edito concidunt homines, exanimantur, quidam vero vivi stupent, et in totum sibi excidunt, quos vocamus attonitos, quorum mentes sonus ille caelestis loco pepulit,: aures,; : talibus attonitus visis ac voce deorum,: attonitus tanto miserarum turbine rerum,; ; ; 9, 409 and 574; 11, 127; 8, 681 al.: alii novitate ac miraculo attoniti, Liv 1, 47; 2, 12; 5, 46; 3, 68 fin.; 7, 36; 30, 30; 39, 15; 44, 10: subitae rei miraculo attoniti,; so ; 3, 13. —With de: mentis de lodice parandā Attonitae,crazed, bewildered about getting a bed-blanket,.—Also without an abl.: Attonitae manibusque uterum celare volenti, Ov M. 2, 463: mater ... Attonitae diu similis fuit,; 6, 600; 12, 498: ut integris corporibus attoniti conciderent,: attoniti vultus,: circumspectare inter se attoniti,: attonitis etiam victoribus,: attonitā magis quam quietā contione,: attonitis jam omnibus,; ; : attonitos habes oculos,; .—Poet., with gen.: attonitus serpentis equus,.—Also poet. transf. to inanimate things: neque enim ante dehiscent Attonitae magna ora domūs, (but acc. to Serv. in an act. sense, syn. with attonitos facientes, stupendae, stunning, terrifying, as pallida senectus, etc.): mensa,: arces, Drak.: quorundam persuasiones,. —
Seized with inspiration, smitten with prophetic fury, inspired, frantic: attonitae Baccho matres,: Bacchus attonitae tribuit vexilla catervae,: Vates, * .—* Adv.: attŏnĭtē, frantically, etc.: Britannia hodieque eum attonite celebrat etc., (Jan, attonita).

Of the mind or manners, agitation (like that of the sea, v. ater and atrocitas maris, ), tumult rage, savageness, barbarity,atrocity, cruelty, roughness: ego quod in hac causā vehementior sum, non atrocitate animi moveor (quis enim est me mitior?) sed, etc.,: hae litterae invidiosam atrocitatem verborum habent, id. ad. Q. Fr. 1, 2, 2, § 6. So, morum,: consilium nefandae atrocitatis,.—In phil. and jurid. lang. severity, harshness: atrocitas ista quo modo in veterem Academiam irruperit, nescio,: atrocitas formularum,the rigid strictness of judicial formulas, Spald.—In plur., , c. 28, p. 252.

Drak.: nec publicanus atterit (Germanos),exhausts, drains,: famam atque pudorem,: et vincere inglorium et atteri sordidum arbitrabatur,and to suffer injury in his dignity, Rupert.: eo tempore, quo praecipue alenda ingenia atque indulgentiā quādam enutrienda sunt, asperiorum tractatu rerum atteruntur,are enfeebled,: filii ejus atterentur egestate,: Nec res atteritur longo sufflamine litis,.— Hence, attrītus, a, um, P. a., rubbed off, worn off or away, wasted.

la:verb:attenuo.html:
at-tĕnŭo (adt-, Lachm., Merk., Weissenb.; att-, Kayser, K. and H., L. Müller), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to make thin or weak; to thin, attenuate; to weaken, enfeeble; to lessen, diminish.
Lit.: aëna Signa manus dextras ostendunt adtenuari Saepe salutantūm tactu, * (cf.: attritum mentum,): bellum (servile) exspectatione Pompeii attenuatum atque imminutum est, adventu sublatum ac sepultum,: legio proeliis attenuata,: diutino morbo viribus admodum adtenuatis,; : fame attenuari,; : macie attenuari,: sortes adtenuatae,diminished,: foliorum exilitate usque in fila attenuatā,: (lingua) attenuans lambendo cutem homines,: Non falx attenuat frondatorum arboris umbram,: adtenuant juvenum vigilatae corpora noctes, (cf. infra, P. a.): patrias opes,; so .—
Trop.: curas lyrā,; : luctus,: insignem attenuat deus,brings low, abases,: attenuabit omnes deos terrae,: hujusmodi partes sunt virtutis amplificandae, si suadebimus; attenuandae, si ab his dehortabimur, Auct. ad. : attenuabitur gloria Jacob,.—Hence, attĕnŭātus (adt-), a, um, P. a., enfeebled, weakened, reduced, weak.
Lit.: adtenuatus amore,: continuatione laborum, August. ap. : fortuna rei familiaris attenuatissima, Auct. ad : voce paululum attenuatā,with a voice a little suppressed,: acuta atque attenuata nimis acclamatio,.—Comp. not in use. —Sup.: fortunae familiares attenuatissimae, Auct. ad .—
Trop.
Feeble, destitute, poor (eccl. Lat.): Siattenuatus frater tuus vendiderit etc.,; ; ; Esdr. 5, 18. —
Esp., of discourse.
Shortened, brief: ipsa illa [pro Roscio] juvenilis redundantia

multa habet attenuata, .—

Too much refined, affected: itaque ejus oratio nimiā religione attenuata doctis et attente audientibus erat illustris,hence his discourse was so delicately formed, through excessive scrupulousness,.—
Meagre, dry, without ornament: attenuata (oratio) est, quae demissa est usque ad usitatissimam puri sermonis consuetudinem, Auct. ad : attenuata verborum constructio,.—* Adv.: at-tenuātē, simply: attenuate presseque dicere,.
